List of Members on Team: Hayden Flo, Sean Ferris, Aritra Gomes, Emma Bradley

I. BACKGROUND
The focus of our research was on determining which systems are critical in evolving the SS Tuffy
from an uncrewed - open, remote-controlled vessel to a boat that is suitable to compete in the uncrewed autonomous division. The past year's iteration of the SS Tuffy established a functional hull and a good
baseline for propulsion and cooling. However, to transition into the autonomous division for the PEP26
competition, this required a full shift in the design and mechanical build of the SS Tuffy.
In order to meet the much higher power draw and the more complex control system needed for an
autonomous vessel, we would need to remove most of the original components. From our research, an
efficient and powerful autonomous system requires high-performance computing to function as the brain,
precise actuation for movement of the vessel, an efficient powertrain, and robust connectivity and sensing
capabilities. Our vessel would need to be designed around these key areas. The only original components
that we deemed suitable to function in our design were the core drivetrain, which consisted of the two TP
5680 brushless motors, the ZTW Seal G2 300A ESCs, the rudder servo, and the propeller shafts.
Additionally, we found that the radiators on the head of the original boat utilized for cooling were
sufficient. Aside from these, everything else needed to be taken out.
The most important part of any autonomous system is the “brain” that controls it. Our design
would need an upgraded flight controller that allows for real-time GPS waypoint following and
MAVLink telemetry for our boat to be continually monitored, controlled, and managed by a humanoperated command center [1]. Not only does the flight controller process the boat's mission data after
receiving telemetry data, but it also receives the data being sent from the battery monitoring system
(BMS) to ensure safe and optimal power performance from our battery. Last year's team utilized the
Holybro Kakute H7, a budget-friendly flight controller that was effective for simple remote control
operations. However, considering the complex processing that our autonomous vessel would demand, we
opted to upgrade to the CubePilot Cube Orange flight controller, which has a superior processor, tripleredundant vibration-isolated IMUs, better modularity, a failsafe processor, and so much more, making it
perfect for an autonomous boat.
In addition to the flight controller, which acts as the vessel's intelligence, an autonomous system
needs to have spatial awareness of where it is located and where it's moving next. This is especially
difficult for marine vessels, with water currents, wind, and other external factors forcibly moving a boat's
heading [2]. Accurate calculation of the vessel's precise latitude, longitude, and altitude is constantly
performed by a high-quality GPS, establishing it as a critical element for tracking. Furthermore, the GPS
captures the vessel's speed, which is critical for a race like the PEP26 competition. Paired with this are the
transmit (Tx) and receive (Rx) antennas that capture and send radio frequency (RF) signals to and from
the flight controller to the remote control. This is critical for observing GPS data as well as taking control
of the boat if needed.
To make a high-endurance and fast autonomous system, a strong power supply is required. To
meet these demands, we constructed a custom 14s7p lithium-ion battery pack, which can handle the high
discharge requirements of the propulsion system while maintaining safe operation of all other
components.
While the SS Tuffy utilizes a pre-existing hull and some original propulsion and cooling
components, the system architecture is entirely original. Every critical subsystem, including power

generation, logic processing, thermal management, and environmental sealing, has been researched,
designed, and integrated by the current team. This project represents a total conversion from a humandependent vehicle to a self-contained, decision-making maritime robot capable of competing at a national
level.

II. Design & Fabrication Process of Sub-Systems
Battery Pack Design & Fabrication:
The battery system was designed to meet the high power and current demands of the vessel’s electric
propulsion system while maintaining efficiency, safety, and structural compatibility with the hull. Initial
research focused on evaluating multiple lithium-ion cell options based on current, capacity, weight, and
cost. Our model for last year used Sanyo NCR18650GA cells in a 14s10p arrangement, but this
configuration was determined to be insufficient, as its maximum continuous current output of
approximately 100 A and total power output of around 5 kW did not meet the propulsion requirements, as
our motors were capable of handling 150 A each, which could provide us with better speed. As a result,
higher-performance cells were investigated, including several Molicel models and the Ampace JP40
21700 cell.
The Ampace JP40 cell was ultimately selected due to its superior current capability and power density. In
a 14s7p configuration, this battery system provides a nominal voltage of approximately 51.8 V, a total
capacity of 28 Ah, and a continuous current capability of up to 490 A, corresponding to a power output of
approximately 25.4 kW. Although the system is capable of delivering significantly higher current, it is not
intended to operate at its maximum rating. Instead, the design targets an operating current of
approximately 300 A. Additionally, the reduced number of cells compared to previous designs lowers the
total system weight and simplifies packaging within the hull.
The electrical design of the battery system emphasizes safe and efficient current distribution. Due to the
high current requirements, traditional nickel strips were deemed inadequate for conducting the required
load. Based on material conductivity analysis, nickel was estimated to carry approximately 5 A/mm²,
while copper can safely carry significantly higher current densities. To address this, the design
incorporates pure nickel strips for series connections and nickel-plated copper strips for parallel cell-level
connections and two thick copper busbars at each end for primary current pathways. Additionally,
multiple spot welds are used at each connection point to distribute current and prevent localized
overheating.

Figure 1: Battery cell Welding Layout

Figure 2: Battery Pack Layouts
Several mechanical configurations were evaluated to integrate the battery system within the hull while
optimizing performance characteristics such as stability, accessibility, and space utilization. Rectangular
layouts offered simplicity and low center of gravity but consumed significant internal space. Vertical
configurations improved cooling and space efficiency but raised the center of gravity, negatively
impacting stability. Alternative layouts, including perpendicular and zig-zag configurations, introduced
trade-offs in accessibility, complexity, and thermal performance. After evaluating multiple battery
mounting configurations, a horizontal rectangular pack design was selected as the final solution. In this
configuration, the battery pack is oriented such that its longest side runs parallel to the length of the hull.
This layout allows the battery to sit low within the vessel, minimizing the center of gravity and improving
overall stability during operation. Additionally, the horizontal arrangement simplifies electrical
connections by allowing straight, accessible busbar routing and more organized wiring between cells, the
BMS, and the propulsion system. Compared to more complex configurations such as the V-shaped layout,
this design reduces assembly complexity, improves accessibility for maintenance, and minimizes the risk
of wiring errors. While this configuration occupies more longitudinal space within the hull, the tradeoff is
justified by improved structural simplicity, reliability, and ease of integration with the mounting system.
Overall, the horizontal battery pack design provides a balanced solution that prioritizes stability,
serviceability, and robust electrical connections.

Figure 3: Final design showing Blown-up Battery assembly
A battery management system (BMS) is connected to the busbar assembly to monitor cell voltages and
ensure safe operation. We are using the Daly 100 Balance 500Amp BMS. Careful consideration is given

Overall Power System Design and Fabrication:

Figure 5: Wiring Diagram
The Power system is designed to ensure safe, reliable distribution of high current from the battery pack to
all propulsion and auxiliary components. The 14s7p battery pack supplies power through a central battery
management system (BMS), which regulates discharge, monitors cell health, and provides system-level
protection. From the BMS, power is distributed to two electronic Seal Series 300A ESCs, each driving a
TP5680 motor. To protect against overcurrent or short-circuit conditions, each ESC is individually fused
with a 200 A ANL fuse, ensuring that a fault in one branch does not propagate through the entire system.
A key safety feature of the design is the inclusion of an external physical switch connected to the BMS
ignition (key) line, allowing operators to immediately disable the entire electrical system from outside the
hull in the event of an emergency. In addition, the system incorporates a precharge circuit that is also
controlled via an external switch. This precharge circuit uses resistors to gradually charge the input

A key safety feature of the design is the inclusion of an external physical switch connected to the BMS

                                                                                                           5

pages.text:
6
capacitors of the ESCs before the main power connection is engaged, preventing large inrush currents that
could damage components or cause connector arcing. Once the system is safely precharged, the main
circuit can be activated. In addition to the high-power propulsion circuitry, the system includes a
dedicated low-power distribution network to safely operate control electronics and auxiliary components.
This low-power circuit is protected by a 5 A fuse, which serves as a primary safeguard against
overcurrent conditions that could damage sensitive components such as the receiver, GPS module,
microcontroller, and sensors. By isolating the low-power system from the high-current propulsion path,
this design prevents faults in auxiliary electronics from impacting critical propulsion functionality.
Furthermore, the DC-DC buck converters used to step down voltage for these subsystems include built-in
overcurrent and thermal protection, providing an additional layer of safety and redundancy. This layered
protection approach ensures that low-power electronics remain stable and protected under varying load
conditions, while also preventing cascading failures between high-power and control systems.

Cooling System Design and Fabrication:

Figure 6: Cooling System Diagram
The thermal management system for the SS Tuffy utilizes an integrated air-and-liquid-cooling design
optimized for high-performance autonomy. The rationale behind this configuration addresses two critical
maritime engineering challenges: the thermal dissipation of high-density battery packs (14s7p) and the
environmental sealing of sensitive electronics. A purely passive system would be insufficient for the
internal heat loads generated.
The cooling system is designed to keep critical components, including the ESCs and battery, within safe
operating temperatures during high-current operation. Since the system is expected to run around 300 A,
significant heat is generated, especially in the ESCs, making thermal management a key part of the
design. To address this, a closed-loop liquid cooling system is used for the ESCs. Coolant is circulated
using dedicated pumps through cooling plates attached to each ESC, allowing heat to be absorbed and
carried away efficiently. The heated coolant is then routed to radiators mounted outside the hull, where
intake fans pull ambient air across the radiator surface to dissipate heat, and exhaust fans push the hot air
out of the system.

In addition to liquid cooling, airflow inside the hull is actively managed using multiple fans to help
regulate the temperature of the battery module and surrounding electronics. These fans direct airflow
across the components, preventing heat buildup in enclosed areas and improving overall cooling
effectiveness. The pumps ensure continuous coolant flow through the system, maintaining consistent heat
transfer from the ESCs to the radiators. This combination of liquid cooling for high-power components
and forced air cooling for the rest of the system provides a balanced and efficient thermal management
solution. Overall, this design reduces the risk of overheating, maintains consistent performance under
load, and improves the reliability and safety of the system during extended operation.

Command and Control System
The command and control subsystem consists of all digital and radio electronics directly responsible for
autonomous planning, position estimation, relaying remote user commands to the craft, relaying of
telemetry data to the user, and propulsion & steering regulation. From the very start, we’ve been very
conscious of the potential dangers that the S.S. Tuffy may pose due to both its large lithium-ion battery
pack and its high target speeds. These two factors mean large amounts of electro-chemical and
mechanical energy are present, energy which could cause grave harm if mismanaged. While designing the
S.S. Tuffy’s command and control subsystem, our core design philosophy has been to maximize
reliability and safety.
With that, we decided to bias our design decisions towards using industry-standard parts and software.
This is because these technologies have already been proven to be safe and reliable by the industry at
large, reducing the risk of dangerous malfunctions. This influenced design decisions to use a CubePilot
CubeOrange as our flight controller, a HolyBro F9P as our water-resistant GPS/compass, ArduRover as
our OS, and MissionPlanner as our ground controller station software. Due to budget limitations, we
weren’t able to replace the SIYI MK15 Transmitter/Receiver system with a more industry-standard
option, but that is a suggestion we have for next year’s team.

from the receiver, whether they be autonomous waypoints or manual inputs. It then uses the parameters
we configured to determine how to translate these inputs into commands to the motors’ electronic speed
controllers and to the rudder servo.
The bluetooth link from the controller to the ground control station laptop allows us to set the S.S. Tuffy’s
autonomous path and view telemetry without any physical connection to the boat. It also enables a
designated team member to focus solely on monitoring the boat’s telemetry data via the ground control
station laptop, ensuring that they can quickly identify problems should they occur.
The GPS/compass module is key to the S.S. Tuffy’s autonomous operation. Our flight controller, with
ArduRover installed, uses the GPS and compass data provided by the module to determine where it is and
what direction it is facing. This estimate is also further refined over time, as ArduRover’s EK3 position
estimation algorithm receives more samples from the GPS/compass module in conjunction with
accelerometer data from the flight controller. While in autonomous mode, ArduRover uses this position
and heading information to determine the forward velocity and heading changes required for the craft to
reach the next target waypoint. The exact amount of throttle and steering applied depends on our
configuration of ArduPilot’s controller gains.

Hull and Physical Design:
The vessel utilizes a 76” × 18” × 14” fiberglass deep-V hull that was retained from the previous design
iteration. This hull was originally selected based on performance calculations and provides good stability,
hydrodynamics, and internal space for system integration. While the external structure remains the same,
the internal layout has been updated to better support the current power and propulsion system. The
propulsion components, including the motors, ESCs, and steering servo, are mounted toward the aft
section of the hull to align with the drive system and maintain proper thrust orientation. The battery
system is positioned slightly forward of the center of gravity to help balance the vessel and improve
stability during operation.

We have a new ballast system design for this year to provide the required 30 lbs of weight to improve
vessel stability and maintain proper trim during operation. To meet the requirement of being removable,
the ballast is constructed using tungsten shot contained within a sealed plastic bag. Tungsten was selected
due to its high density, allowing a significant amount of weight to be concentrated in a compact volume.
The measured 30 lbs of tungsten shot is placed into a gallon-sized plastic bag, which is then filled with
epoxy and sealed to create a solid, durable ballast block. Because the tungsten shot is loose before curing,
the ballast is able to conform to the shape of the hull as the epoxy sets, allowing it to better utilize
otherwise unused space and reduce dead volume within the hull. Once cured, the ballast is positioned at
the bottom of the hull, directly beneath the command and control housing, to lower the center of gravity
and improve overall stability. This placement ensures that the ballast sits securely and evenly, minimizing
movement while also enhancing balance without interfering with other components. Additionally, the
design allows the ballast to be removed or repositioned if adjustments are needed during testing.

The railing system features pieces of metal angle that is epoxied to the side of the hull and raised using
wooden offsets. Metal square extrusion is bolted into holes on the side of the metal angle. These pieces of
extrusion are what holds our battery pack and command and control module. This allows for easy
installation and disassembly of both devices. This system also allows for easy access of the ballast for
removal and measurement before the beginning of the race.

Propulsion System and Propellers
The propulsion system consists of the primary mechanical and electrical components responsible for
generating thrust and controlling the vessel’s motion, including the motors, electronic speed controllers
(ESCs), propellers, and steering mechanisms. The system utilizes dual TP 5680 brushless motors rated at
330 KV, which are retained from the previous design due to their proven performance and reliability.
These motors are paired with ZTW Seal Series 300A G2 ESCs, which provide precise control of motor
speed based on throttle input from the remote control system.
At the selected system voltage of approximately 48–52 V, the 330 KV motors operate at an estimated
speed of around 15,000–16,000 RPM, which aligns well with the ESC operating limits and the desired
propulsion performance. This matching of motor speed and ESC capability ensures efficient operation
without exceeding component ratings. Each ESC is connected to the battery system through a fused
power line for protection and delivers three-phase power directly to the motors, enabling smooth and
responsive torque generation.
The motors transfer rotational energy through the drive shafts to the propellers, which generate thrust to
propel the vessel forward. The system utilizes ABC 3014 two-blade cleaver propellers, which have a
diameter of 3.0 inches (76.2 mm) and a pitch of 4.2 inches (106.68 mm). The relatively large diameter of
this propeller allows for increased thrust generation, making it well-suited for pushing the vessel under
high load conditions. The cleaver-style design is optimized for high-speed surface operation, improving
efficiency and reducing drag at higher speeds. Additionally, the propellers are made from beryllium
copper, which provides high strength and durability under high rotational speeds and loads. These
propellers are designed for a 1/4-inch shaft and are adapted as needed to match the drivetrain
configuration. While these propellers do not come pre-sharpened or balanced, they can be tuned to
improve performance and efficiency during testing. Multiple propeller options are still evaluated to finetune performance characteristics such as thrust, speed, and overall efficiency.

The vessel utilizes an aluminum rudder assembly designed to provide precise and reliable steering control
at high speeds. The rudder is mounted to a reinforced bracket and actuated through a servo-driven linkage
system, allowing accurate angular positioning based on user input. Its streamlined shape minimizes drag
while maintaining effective water deflection for directional control. The rigid aluminum construction
ensures durability and consistent performance under high loads and dynamic operating conditions.
Steering is achieved using the servo-driven rudder system. The servo receives control signals from the
flight controller, which interprets user input from the remote control. This motion is transferred through a
push-rod linkage to actuate the rudders, allowing precise directional control of the vessel.

To validate the performance of the electrical and control systems, testing was conducted to evaluate
current draw and system stability across the expected operating voltage range. The command and control
system was tested using a variable power supply from 30 V to 55 V to simulate real operating conditions.
The measured current draw remained consistent at approximately 0.25–0.26 A across all voltages,
indicating stable and efficient operation of components such as the flight controller, receiver, and sensors.
This low current draw confirms that the control system places minimal load on the overall power system.
Additional testing was performed on the DC-DC converter used to step down the voltage for low-power
components. The converter was evaluated across an input range of 30 V to 60 V and showed an output
current of approximately 2.4 µA under no-load conditions. This demonstrates very low standby power
consumption and high efficiency when the system is idle.
Overall, the results confirm that the low-power system is stable, efficient, and well-integrated with the
overall power system. The consistent performance across voltage ranges ensures reliable operation
without significantly impacting battery usage.

III. Risks
The inherent risks with this vessel come from the volatility of the battery cells and the power that can be
delivered to the propulsion system. LiPo battery cells are temperature sensitive and require a specific
range of charge voltage. The propulsion system operating metal propellers at a maximum rotational speed
of 16,000 RPM poses a risk when these components are given power at an incorrect time (i.e. during
servicing and maintenance).

Battery Pack Risk Mitigation
The battery system is in line with a robust BMS and several fuses to protect the rest of the system from
any battery malfunction. The cells themselves are sealed and raised above the bottom of the hull in case
any water breaches the hull.
The fuses ensure that all possible routes for fault current are protected. Both ESCs are protected by
200Amp fuses. While both ESCs are capable of handling a much greater amperage, the associated heat
that would be produced by these components would not be properly compensated by the cooling system.
The Command and Control system is protected by several, low amperage fuses to protect these
components from the high voltage/amperage cables that will be run adjacent to their container. The BMS
system itself contains an internal current-cutoff that will protect the system if any current above 400Amps
is ever drawn from the array. If this event occurs, the BMS opens the internal power MOSFETs to protect
the system.
The battery pack is physically separated from the surface of the hull using our railing system. The battery
pack container is made of PLA treated with acetone to ensure all surfaces are waterproof. In the case of a
water leak-caused battery fault, there is an emergency shut-off switch that will allow for the safe
extraction of the battery pack. The cells are temperature-controlled with a temperature-based shutoff.

Autonomous Risk Mitigation
The remote controller can manually switch the flight controller between autonomous mode and manual
mode to aid in recovering the craft during testing, which is especially helpful in the event of an error
while in autonomous mode. Alternatively, in the event of an emergency, the craft can be similarly
switched into “Hold” mode, where all motors will brake to a stop, and the rudder servo won’t move.

In addition to these crucial manual safety measures, ArduRover supports several automated failsafe
measures, all of which we have enabled on the S.S. Tuffy and all of which put it into “Hold” mode when
triggered. Specifically, we have enabled the “Ground Control Station”, “Throttle”, “EKF”, and “Crash
Detection” failsafe conditions. The “Ground Control Station” condition triggers if the craft has not
received communication from the ground control station for at least 2 seconds (the minimum configurable
timeout duration). The “Throttle” failsafe condition triggers if the received throttle signal over RF is
lower than the minimum possible actual throttle input, indicating that the remote controller is too far away
to properly send commands. The “EKF” failsafe triggers under the loss of critical position sensors,
especially including the GPS. The “Crash Detection” failsafe triggers when the pitch or roll of the craft
exceeds 45 degrees, which would indicate that the craft is capsized or similar.
